title: Mobility as a Public Function of Common Interest: Reframing Metropolitan Governance Through Comparative Evidence From London And Brazilian Metropolitan Regions
content: Metropolitan regions have become the dominant spatial form of urbanisation in the twenty-first century, yet their governance structures remain poorly aligned with the functional dynamics that sustain them. Among these dynamics, mobility plays a central but paradoxical role: while it structures daily life, economic integration and territorial cohesion, it is still predominantly treated as a sectoral transport policy rather than as a core public function of metropolitan governance. This article reframes mobility as a Public Function of Common Interest (FPIC) and examines how its institutional recognition, or absence, shapes metropolitan governance and sustainability outcomes. Drawing on a comparative mixed-methods analysis of Greater London and two Brazilian metropolitan regions (Porto Alegre and Serra Gaúcha), the study develops an analytical framework linking mobility, governance capacity and metropolitan sustainability. The findings demonstrate that differences in mobility outcomes are less a function of economic development or technological capacity than of institutional design, coordination mechanisms and governance continuity. By positioning mobility as an organising principle of metropolitan governance, the article advances international debates on sustainable urban regions and offers a transferable analytical framework for metropolitan policy and planning.
